items.title: If you can't test, add a holding dose
items.because: If you can't test today, 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine raises free chlorine by about 1.5 ppm. That is a holding dose, not a shock: 2 ppm is below what you would swim in, so it cannot over-chlorinate the pool, and it buys a day without pretending to know what the level actually is. Test before adding any more than this.
items.why: ORP is 419 mV and free chlorine wasn't measured, so you don't know if the water is sanitizing. This small liquid chlorine dose is a holding measure: it lifts free chlorine without risking over-chlorination, but only use it if you can't test today.
items.how: Make sure the pump is running before anything goes in, and keep it running afterward. Pour the 0.25 gal of 12.5% liquid chlorine slowly around the deep end, standing at the edge, and keep it away from any bucket that has had acid in it. Never mix chlorine and acid in the same container.

items.title: Test free chlorine today
items.because: ORP is 419 mV, well under the 550 mV mark where the water may genuinely not be sanitising. Free chlorine isn't measured -- the ICO can't read it -- so nobody knows whether that is a real chlorine shortage or just the proxy sagging. Salt is out of band, which depresses ORP on its own, so this may resolve once it is fixed. It is still worth a strip test today rather than assuming.
items.why: ORP is 419 mV, under the 600 mV target, but the ICO can't read free chlorine, so this could be a real chlorine shortage or just low salt dragging ORP down. Free chlorine is not measured, and a strip test is the only way to tell which it is.
items.how: Dip a fresh strip in water taken from elbow depth, away from the return jet, with the pump running. Compare the free chlorine pad against the 2 ppm minimum right away. The result decides whether the holding dose is needed.

items.title: Add salt
items.because: Salt is 1,098 ppm, below the 2800-3200 ppm the cell needs. A cell run under its salt band makes less chlorine and wears out faster.
items.why: Salt is 1,098 ppm against a 2,800–3,200 band, and a cell under its band makes less chlorine and wears out faster. That low salt is the likely reason ORP is at 419 mV.
items.how: Run the pump and pour the salt in around the deep end in portions, brushing it around so it dissolves instead of sitting in a pile. Because this is a vinyl liner, don't let salt settle on the floor, and keep the pump running afterward so it disperses. Salt can't be predissolved in a bucket in practice at this volume, so keep brushing until the granules are gone.

dose.label: 90 lb of salt (about 2.25 of a 40 lb bag)

items.title: Empty the skimmer basket
items.because: Last emptied 4 days ago; the cadence is every 3.
items.why: The skimmer basket was last emptied 4 days ago and the cadence is every 3. A full basket restricts flow, and with the cell only making chlorine while water moves through it, you want flow unrestricted.
items.how: Leave the pump running and lift the basket out by the handle. Dump the debris away from the pool and rinse the basket before dropping it back in.

items.title: Leave the cell alone for now
items.because: ORP is 419 mV, under the at least 600 mV floor -- but Salt is out of band too, and ORP sits downstream of all of it. Fix that first, give the water a full day to circulate, then re-read. Turning the cell up now just means running it harder against the same problem.
items.why: ORP is 419 mV against a floor of at least 600, but salt is also out of band and ORP follows from it. Turning the cell up now only makes it work harder against the same problem.
items.how: Don't touch the cell settings today. Add the salt, let the water circulate for a full day with the pump running, then take a fresh reading.

items.title: The cell is already flat out
items.because: The cell is at 100% (from config.json), running 24 hours a day, so there is no headroom left to ask for -- this is not a setting you can turn up. Salt is out of band, and each of those starves the cell in its own way: low salt gives it less to work with, high pH wastes the chlorine it makes, low CYA lets the sun burn it off. Fix those and the same cell will produce more.
items.why: The cell is already at 100% and running 24 hours a day, so there is nothing left to turn up. Salt at 1,098 ppm is starving it, and fixing that is what will get more chlorine out of the same cell.
items.how: Leave the cell output at 100% and don't change anything on the controller. The salt addition is the move that helps.

items.title: Leave the pump schedule alone for now
items.because: The pump is running 24 hours a day, which is a lot -- but on a saltwater pool the pump schedule is the chlorine schedule, because the cell only makes chlorine while water is going through it. With ORP at 419 mV, cutting hours would cut production exactly when you need it. Get ORP comfortably over 600 with the cell below full, and that is the moment to start trimming hours and watching what happens.
items.why: The pump runs 24 hours a day, but on a saltwater pool that schedule is the chlorine schedule since the cell only makes chlorine while water flows through it. With ORP at 419 mV, cutting hours would cut chlorine when you need it most.
items.how: Leave the timer as it is. Once ORP is comfortably over 600 and the cell is below full, that is the time to start trimming hours.

items.title: Test borates
items.because: Borates aren't on the ICO panel and haven't been tested. The target is 50 ppm; a strip test once a season is enough to know where you are.
items.why: Borates haven't been measured and the target is 50 ppm. A single strip test per season is enough to know where you stand.
items.how: Take a sample from elbow depth with the pump running and use a borate test strip or kit. Record the number so it's on file for the season.

safety_rules: NEVER pour undiluted acid into the skimmer. Acid down the skimmer runs neat through the pump, heater and salt cell and eats them. Dilute it and pour it slowly around the deep end with the pump running.

NEVER put shock and acid in the same session without at least 4 hours between them, and say the gap out loud in the instructions. Both move pH hard in opposite directions, and back to back you cannot tell what the water actually did.
ALWAYS predissolve dry chemicals in a 5-gallon bucket of pool water before they go in. Undissolved granules sitting on a vinyl liner bleach and weaken it.
NEVER put chlorine and acid in the same bucket, in either order. That combination produces chlorine gas.
ALWAYS add acid to water, never water to acid -- pouring water into acid can boil and spit it back at you.
The pump must be RUNNING before anything goes in, and keep running afterwards, so a dose disperses instead of sitting in one corner.
headline: Salt is far too low and ORP is sagging; test chlorine, add salt, hold with a small dose
summary: The reading is fresh from today. Salt is 1,098 ppm against a 2,800–3,200 band and ORP is 419 mV against at least 600, so the cell is working with too little salt. Free chlorine, CYA, TA and borates weren't measured, so test chlorine first and treat the rest as unknown.
